title: Floating Iron, Hidden Armies, Starving City
overview: Elisha helps his students, protects Israel from Aramean raiders, spares an enemy army, and is blamed by Israel's king when a long siege brings famine to Samaria.

parts.label: The floating axhead (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: A growing group of prophets in training builds a bigger meeting place by the Jordan River, and one of them loses a borrowed iron axhead in the water. Iron was costly and he likely could not repay it, so Elisha throws in a stick and the iron floats up.

parts.label: Elisha exposes enemy plans (vv. 8-12)
parts.note: Aram, a kingdom roughly where Syria is today, keeps raiding Israel, but Elisha keeps warning Israel's king where the raiders will strike. Aram's king suspects a traitor and is told the prophet knows even what he says in his bedroom.

parts.label: An army of fire (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: Aram sends a whole army by night to Dothan, a town north of Samaria, to capture one man. Elisha's terrified servant is allowed to see the hills full of fiery horses and chariots, a picture of God's unseen protection around the prophet.

parts.label: Enemies fed, not killed (vv. 18-23)
parts.note: The soldiers are struck blind, which may mean confused rather than fully sightless, and Elisha leads them into Samaria, Israel's capital. On Elisha's word the king feeds them and sends them home instead of killing them, and the raids stop.

parts.label: Siege and famine (vv. 24-29)
parts.note: During Ben-Hadad's siege, a donkey's head, food the law counted unclean, sells for a fortune, and so does a tiny measure of some cheap food whose exact identity scholars are unsure of. A mother tells the king that she and another woman agreed to eat their sons, the horror that the warnings in Deuteronomy said a siege could bring.

parts.label: The king blames Elisha (vv. 30-33)
parts.note: The king tears his robes to reveal sackcloth, rough cloth worn in grief or repentance, yet swears to have Elisha beheaded, perhaps because the prophet had urged him to hold out. Elisha knows the king's men are coming, and the chapter ends with bitter words that this disaster comes from the LORD, so why wait for him any longer.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the fiery army around Elisha promises similar unseen protection to believers today or describes a special moment tied to Elisha's role.
think: Elisha has the soldiers who came to capture him fed and sent home, and the raids stop; when, if ever, have you seen kindness toward an opponent change things more than force could have?
